analysis.one_liner: Orders the commodities regulator to curb excessive speculation that inflates energy prices.
analysis.headline: The bill to curb oil market speculation never got a hearing or vote; it died in the House Agriculture Committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, within 14 days of passage, to use its existing and emergency powers to curb excessive speculation in energy futures and swap markets — the financial trading that the bill argues drives up gasoline prices beyond what supply and demand justify. It cites a Goldman Sachs estimate that speculation added roughly 56 cents to the price of a gallon of gasoline, and notes that in early 2012 gasoline hit a record March price even though oil supply was up and demand was down.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who buys gasoline, heating oil, or other energy products, if speculation is in fact pushing prices above what supply and demand would set. Airlines, trucking companies, and other businesses that buy large amounts of fuel would also benefit from prices that track actual supply and demand.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and everyone who buys fuel

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the CFTC, within 14 days of enactment, to use its authority — including emergency powers — to immediately curb excessive speculation in markets trading energy futures and swaps, and to eliminate price distortion and unwarranted price swings [S2] [S3].

The bill cites CFTC Chairman Gary Gensler's 2011 testimony that 80 to 87 percent of the oil futures market is dominated by financial participants — swap dealers, hedge funds, and other financials — a share that had more than doubled over the prior decade [S3].

It cites data showing prices detached from fundamentals: in late 2011 world oil supply rose by 1.3 million barrels a day while demand rose only 700,000, yet crude prices rose over 12 percent, and in March 2012 gasoline hit the highest March price on record even though U.S. gasoline demand was lower than in 1997 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hedge funds, swap dealers, and other financial firms that profit from large speculative positions in energy markets would lose a trading strategy if the CFTC cracked down. Energy traders argue that speculation adds liquidity to markets, though the bill's findings dispute that this benefits consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hedge funds and energy swap dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill rests on contested evidence: its headline figure — a 56-cent-per-gallon speculation premium — comes from a newspaper article citing a Goldman Sachs analysis, and economists disagree about how much financial speculation, rather than supply and demand, drives energy prices [S3].

The mandate is broad and immediate: it directs the CFTC to act within 14 days using emergency powers to eliminate 'excessive' speculation without sharply defining that term, which critics could argue hands the regulator wide discretion to intervene in markets on short notice [S3].

If speculation adds less to pump prices than the bill claims, the cost would be reduced market liquidity for energy hedgers — airlines and fuel buyers use these markets to lock in prices — without a matching benefit to consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's findings are right, the benefit is large and broad: cheaper gasoline for every household and business, at a cost only to financial traders. If the economists who dispute the speculation premium are right, the bill is a heavy-handed intervention with little consumer payoff. The honest reading is that the evidence on how much speculation raises pump prices is genuinely contested, but the bill targeted a real, documented problem — financial participants dominating oil futures markets — with an unusually blunt deadline.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2012 and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on April 19, 2012, with 28 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction, and on May 10, 2012, to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management — the committee with jurisdiction over the CFTC [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms trading energy futures — hedge funds, swap dealers, and other speculators — kept their positions and strategies intact, since the bill died before any position limits or emergency actions it demanded could take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Speculative energy traders kept their market positions

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the CFTC to curb excessive energy speculation, citing record March gasoline prices despite ample supply.

for.name: 28 of 28 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 28 were Democrats.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired during the 112th Congress by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and referred it to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 supporters — the sponsor and 28 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the bill never reached a floor vote where any Republican position would have been recorded [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Energy futures traders (hedge funds, swap dealers, index funds)
industries.note: These financial participants held 80 to 87 percent of the oil futures market, and the bill would have required the CFTC to immediately curb their role and impose position limits. Their gain comes from trading strategies the bill's findings say add a premium to what consumers pay at the pump, so their interest runs against drivers' [S3].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and marketers
industries.note: The bill does not regulate producers directly, but if speculation premiums were removed, prices received for oil and gasoline would likely fall toward supply-and-demand levels — a cost to sellers and a gain to buyers. High prices benefit producers, so their interest in this bill runs against consumers' [S3].
